author: @masegodipela
text:
It is very obvious that they are ignoring clear differences between live battles and the battle we are witnessing. 

1. The dimension of time. With the Kdot/Drake battle, we actually have time in-between responses to go digest and research; so ambiguous lines give us something to do while waiting for the next response. 

2. Still on the dimension of time, in a live battle, the audience needs to react immediately to what you said, so it has to be more direct. 

3. Lastly, your oponent could possibly take weeks to respond to you so you have to be very clever about how you set up your knock out track, or you might give your opponent the opportunity to change strategies. 

There is a lot more to say, but I believe you guys should be tapped in to all the demensions of this battle. Its not a live battle its playing out over months now.

author: @daShadoSage
text:
This is all twisted. It's as if they're deep into an analysis of boxing rules and judging, but they're watching MMA. Or explaining pick up basketball but watching Olympics level. This. Isn't. Battle. Rap.


This isn't freestyles on one mic on unknown or usually zero beats with a live audience screaming “Ooohhhh”.  


Round by round? That's not what it is. I mean it doesn't even make sense at the pace Drizzy and K Dot are going. I don't know what they say later as the beef goes on but you don't do rounds like it's Battle rap as anyone can release as many records as they want at any time. Happened with Meek Mill as well who released multiple tracks back to back but no one bothered. In fact Drake won based really on one song. Just like Pusha T won based on one song with different rules that were spontaneously established.


They're here comparing Like That of a single indirect verse that was a call to the fight and comparing it to a full throated (No Diddy) response song from Drake 23 days later. Again they're trying so hard and so wrong to fit a square peg in a round hole bringing up Battle rap freestyle on zero beats from very very unknown rappers (commercially). Didn't even bother talking about the history of actual commercial level diss rapping and music. K Dot is setting up an entire musical epic. 6:16 was an interlude that came after K Dot's own song Euphoria. These guys try to apply Battle rap rules which makes zero sense here. They're not in the right field. Feels like watching new judges coming from amateur boxing trying to explain what they see happening in high level MMA. 


Lastly, they're talking about direct bars. Or at least they're saying that's what they are doing. Push Ups didn't have much at K Dot. They're so confused that even the rules they think they're applying they're really not. In Battle Rap it's 99% one on one with a person right in front of you. Drake spent a huge portion of the Push Ups (and later Family Matters) talking to 5+ other dudes not even in the ‘room’ or off their couch. His most memorable line was against a damn producer with zero complexity or scheme or bar. But it was funny. It worked musically. But in Battle rap that's a 0. But good thing this isn't Battle rap. But again apply their incorrect rules. Strip that away, strip any bar not at K Dot, drop the musical elements, drop any singing, drop the bridges and the choruses. Battle rap has none of that. Then what's left?? Not much and something that would fail in Battle rap (does that mean every single person [ironically Drake even called out a basketball player] Drake mentioned but who didn't reply [yet] automatically lose? Did Kanye “win” because of Like That freestyle response? Did Rick Rowin "win” bacause he had a full response with Champagne Moments?). But together, it works as what it was meant to be, a diss song that works musically with some bars and light punches. A more direct diss record that should be more compared to Euphoria side by side if you felt so compelled to do a side by side comparison. Still unfocused enough for me as a diss record but very much a worthy contribution to the epic.

Country had their Drakes too... one of the first was Fiddlin' John Carson who went to Atlanta and became the face of music written by Black artists, talking about running moonshine and other content that wasn't true to his experience. He was the guy Charlie Daniels spoke about in "The Devil Went Down to Georgia." And the rest is history. They didn't have rules in place to keep him from earning respect on a strategic lie. Now, they look at Beyoncé sideways for standing on their stage.

It's not that Kendrick is good or that Drake is evil but the impact that each of them will ultimately have on hip hop and culture at large... there is actually no comparison. One leads to Black erasure from hip hop just as it has in every genre of music. Rap has been somewhat protected by all the rules Drake has been allowed to openly break while keeping his position at the top. Now, we have prominent people in hip hop publicly saying they don't mind if Drake is using writers and that he is still winning "even if he didn't write it". *That* is Drake's legacy.
